notes: PPC permit JR for Rugby cement works; disclosure failure on Aqmau reports but relief refused on discretion.

enrichment.short_title: Edwards v Environment Agency: PPC permit and tyre-burning judicial review

statutes_considered.title: Pollution Prevention and Control (England and Wales) Regulations 2000

key_facts: The Environment Agency granted a PPC permit in August 2003 allowing Rugby cement works to trial burning chipped tyres as fuel.
Mr Edwards challenged the decision by judicial review, initially focusing on tyre burning but later on PM10 particulate emissions from low-level pollution sources.
Internal Aqmau air-dispersion reports were used in the decision but not disclosed to consultees before the permit was granted.
The claim succeeded on a fairness/disclosure ground but Lindsay J refused to quash the permit in his discretion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of an Environment Agency PPC permit decision after permission was granted by Keith J.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to apply granted; substantive challenge largely failed; Aqmau non-disclosure was unlawful but the permit and decision document were not quashed; no ECJ reference.
enrichment.ratio: Fair consultation may require disclosure of internal expert reports that are likely to influence a pollution-control decision, but quashing remains discretionary where no substantive breach of air-quality requirements is shown and other remedies exist.
legal_issues: Whether tyre burning or continued operation required an environmental impact assessment
Whether internal Aqmau reports should have been disclosed before the PPC decision
Whether the Agency misunderstood air-dispersion material in its decision document
Whether relief should be refused despite procedural unfairness
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Environment ex parte Bushell [1981] AC 75
R (on the application of Capenhurst) v Leicester City Council [2004] EWHC 2124 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Final disposition on each major ground and discretionary refusal of quashing are clearly recorded.

notes: Committal of solicitor for non-delivery of files; dismissed on merits and for defective personal service.

enrichment.short_title: Tankaria v Morgan: committal application for breach of conveyancing order
key_facts: Property developers sued solicitor Miss Morgan for failure to account for conveyancing monies and to deliver client files.
Master Bragge ordered forthwith delivery of documents and verified cash statements by March 2005.
Miss Morgan delivered files late and incompletely; a committal application was served in March 2005.
Laddie J dismissed the application because wilful breach was not proved beyond reasonable doubt and the penal order was not personally served.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application to commit a solicitor for contempt for breach of a Chancery Masters' order in underlying Part 8 proceedings.
enrichment.outcome: Committal application dismissed on both merits and procedural grounds, though the judge strongly criticised Miss Morgan's conduct.
enrichment.ratio: Contempt must be proved beyond reasonable doubt as charged in the application notice at the date of service; mere failure to comply with a mandatory order is insufficient without intentional breach, and an order endorsed with a penal notice must be personally served.
legal_issues: Whether Miss Morgan intentionally breached Master Bragge's order
Whether subsequent compliance could be relied on as part of the charge
Whether personal service of the penal notice was required and satisfied
Whether 'forthwith' delivery allowed the delay alleged

confidence.notes: Findings on intention, service requirements and dismissal are explicit.

notes: Miss World sponsorship dispute; Court of Appeal held RVSG monies were not Gala Dinner profits.

enrichment.short_title: Onyeador v Miss World: proprietary claim to Rivers State sponsorship money
key_facts: Miss Onyeador provided an HSBC bank guarantee so Allianz could stage a Miss World charity gala dinner in London in November 2002.
Rivers State paid US$1m sponsorship to Miss World Ltd via Silverbird, largely to fund the Nigeria pageant rather than the London dinner.
Miss Onyeador claimed 60% of net profits by assignment, subrogation or constructive trust from Allianz against Miss World Ltd.
Judge Reid dismissed the claim against Miss World Ltd; the Court of Appeal upheld that decision.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a six-day Chancery trial before HHJ Robert Reid QC on proprietary and restitutionary claims over sponsorship monies.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the RVSG sponsorship monies were not profits relating to or accruable from the London gala dinner.
enrichment.ratio: Sponsorship paid to discharge obligations under the main pageant agreement cannot fairly be treated as profits of a separate London charity dinner unless the parties to the sponsorship agreement so intended; Allianz had no prior claim and thus Miss Onyeador had none against Miss World Ltd.
legal_issues: Whether Allianz acted as agent of Miss World Ltd in agreements with Miss Onyeador
Whether Miss Onyeador was assignee of Allianz's contractual profit share
Whether RVSG sponsorship monies were net profits of the London gala dinner
Whether subrogation or constructive trust could arise without Allianz's prior claim

confidence.notes: Central preliminary question and unanimous dismissal are clearly reasoned.

notes: Adverse possession claim failed; occupants lacked intention to dispossess believing licence continued.

enrichment.short_title: Clowes v Walters: adverse possession and licensee occupation of farm
key_facts: Clowes Developments sought possession of Boulton Edge Farm, occupied for years under a rent-free licence granted to Mrs Walters.
Claire and Nigel Walters continued living there after Mrs Walters moved out in 1988, believing occupation was permitted by the landowner.
They claimed title by adverse possession from August 1989 when Clowes became registered proprietor.
Hart J held they never intended to dispossess the paper owner and granted possession to Clowes Developments.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Trial of a possession claim resisted on limitation and adverse possession grounds after licence purportedly terminated in 2001.
enrichment.outcome: Claimant entitled to recover possession; defendants' adverse possession defence failed.
enrichment.ratio: A squatter who occupies believing he does so with the paper owner's permission lacks the intention to possess required for adverse possession under the Limitation Act, following Pye v Graham; a constructive trust may preserve a bare licence across transfer of the legal estate.
legal_issues: Whether transfer from Mayfair to Clowes Developments determined Mrs Walters' licence
Whether Claire and Nigel had factual possession and intention to possess
Application of Pye v Graham and BP Properties v Buckler
Whether section 3 Human Rights Act required a different approach to dispossession
linked_authorities: J A Pye (Oxford) Ltd v Graham [2002] UKHL 30
BP Properties Ltd v Buckler (1988) 55 P&CR 337

confidence.notes: Detailed fact findings and clear possession order reasoning.

notes: Case stated on religiously aggravated s5 Public Order offence; magistrates' no case to answer ruling quashed.

enrichment.short_title: DPP v Humphrey: case stated on religiously aggravated public order offence
key_facts: The defendant allegedly said 'You're fucking Islam' and 'Kalima' to a Sikh police constable in Maidstone.
Magistrates found no case to answer on a section 5 religiously aggravated public order charge.
The DPP appealed by case stated arguing the magistrates applied the wrong test and gave flawed reasons.
Leveson J held the words were almost undeniably abusive and quashed the decision, ordering re-hearing.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by way of case stated from Mid-Kent Magistrates' Court against a no-case-to-answer ruling.
enrichment.outcome: Stated case answered in the negative; magistrates' decision quashed and matter remitted for re-hearing before a different bench.
enrichment.ratio: On Galbraith principles magistrates must ask whether a reasonable tribunal could convict; referring to an Asian officer as 'fucking Islam' is capable of being threatening, abusive or insulting and the magistrates' reasons did not justify finding otherwise.
legal_issues: Whether the words were capable of being threatening, abusive or insulting
Whether the magistrates conflated abuse with likelihood of distress
Correct application of the Galbraith no-case-to-answer test
Whether intoxication and confused demeanour negated abuse

confidence.notes: Magistrates' reasons analysed in detail and quashing order clearly made.

notes: Housing benefit subsidy recovery JR; 2004 decision to resume instalments upheld.

enrichment.short_title: Lambeth v SoS: judicial review of resumed housing benefit subsidy recovery
key_facts: Lambeth was overpaid about £31.5 million housing benefit subsidy between 1991/92 and 1996/97 for failing to refer rents to rent officers.
In 1998 the Secretary of State required full recovery over ten years without interest; about £22.5 million had been repaid by 2004.
After Bridgnorth litigation the Department adopted a new discretionary recovery policy in Circular HB/CTB S1/2002.
Lambeth sought to stop further recovery; Stanley Burnton J dismissed the judicial review of the 2004 decision to resume deductions.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Secretary of State's 2004 decision to resume recovery of outstanding pre-1997 housing benefit subsidy overpayments.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the Secretary of State was entitled to adhere to the unchallenged 1998 recovery decision and the new policy did not apply retrospectively.
enrichment.ratio: Section 137(6) recovery of overpaid subsidy is not a penalty but adjustment machinery; a decision to continue implementing an earlier lawful recovery arrangement is reviewable but not perverse where no material change of circumstances warrants revisiting the original decision.
legal_issues: Whether the 2004 decision was a fresh reviewable decision or mere implementation
Whether continued recovery was perverse given loss to the public purse
Whether Circular S1/2002 applied to Lambeth's outstanding debt
Distinction between discretion under section 137(6) and section 140C(3)
linked_authorities: R (Bridgnorth District Council) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2001] (unreported, Sullivan J)
R (Anglesey County Council) v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions [2003] EWHC 2518 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Statutory framework and grounds of challenge addressed comprehensively though some policy context is complex.

notes: Fresh asylum claim refused under rule 346 after IAT rejection; March 2004 Kosovo unrest insufficient.

enrichment.short_title: Hati v SSHD: refusal to treat post-2004 representations as fresh asylum claim

statutes_considered.title: Convention relating to the Status of Refugees 1951

key_facts: Mr Hati, a Gorani from Kosovo, had an asylum claim refused by the IAT in November 2003.
Following March 2004 inter-ethnic violence in Kosovo he submitted further representations said to constitute a fresh claim.
The Secretary of State refused under rule 346, finding the new material insufficiently different to admit a realistic prospect of success.
Gibbs J dismissed judicial review, holding UNHCR reports showed Goranis were not specifically targeted and conditions had stabilised.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of refusal to treat further representations as a fresh asylum application under Immigration Rule 346.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; refusal letters and detailed grounds of defence were lawful and adequately reasoned.
enrichment.ratio: A fresh asylum claim requires a significant change in essential ingredients such that a favourable view is realistically possible despite the earlier rejection; post-IAT unrest affecting Goranis generally, without new personal persecution evidence, does not meet that test.
legal_issues: Application of rule 346 and Onibiyo principles to post-IAT representations
Whether March 2004 Kosovo violence changed essential ingredients of the claim
Proper assessment of UNHCR and Dr Hudson reports
Whether Gorani-specific risk of persecution was shown after the IAT decision
linked_authorities: R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Onibiyo [1996] QB 768
R v Secretary of State for the Home Department ex parte Ravichandran (No 3) [1997] 1 Imm AR 74

confidence.notes: Legal framework and factual assessment of country material are clearly set out.

notes: Bail refusal JR granted; Crown Court decision quashed as Wednesbury unreasonable under Sch 1 para 6.

enrichment.short_title: Wiggins v Harrow Crown Court: judicial review of bail refusal after late attendance
key_facts: The claimant faced affray and imitation firearm charges and had complied with bail until trial day on 21 March 2005.
He arrived about 105 minutes late, saying he had overlooked the trial, and bail was revoked under Bail Act Schedule 1 paragraph 6.
Her Honour Judge Freedman refused further bail despite prior compliance and prosecution non-objection.
Collins J quashed the bail refusal as Wednesbury unreasonable and remitted reconsideration to the Crown Court.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission and substantive hearing of judicial review of a Crown Court refusal to extend bail before trial.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted; decision quashed; matter remitted to Harrow Crown Court for bail to be reconsidered.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 6 Schedule 1 Bail Act prohibits bail after failure to surrender without reasonable cause unless no significant risk of further failure; a single late attendance after long compliance does not reasonably justify fear of future non-surrender, and exceptional intervention on robust Wednesbury review is permitted.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 6 reversed the presumption in favour of bail
Whether forgetting the trial date was reasonable cause
Scope of judicial review of Crown Court bail decisions after Criminal Justice Act 2003
Application of Article 5 ECHR and proportionality at review stage
linked_authorities: M v Isleworth Crown Court [2005] EWHC 363 (Admin)
R (Shergill) v Harrow Crown Court [2005] EWHC 2005 (Admin)

confidence.notes: Bail Act analysis and quashing order are explicit though some trial facts were incomplete.

notes: Homelessness priority need appeal dismissed; Pereira/Osmani vulnerability test correctly applied.

enrichment.short_title: Bellouti v Lambeth: priority need vulnerability under Housing Act 1996
key_facts: Mr Bellouti, a refugee with back pain, depression and diabetes, applied to Wandsworth as homeless with priority need.
The council's independent medical adviser Dr Keen found he could live independently and made no housing recommendation.
The review officer upheld refusal applying the Pereira vulnerability test against ordinary homeless persons.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, applying guidance in Osmani on section 189(1)(c).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from Central London County Court dismissing an appeal against a section 202 review decision on priority need.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; review decision was not Wednesbury unreasonable and no procedural unfairness in relying on Dr Keen's final report.
enrichment.ratio: Vulnerability under section 189(1)(c) is a composite assessment whether, when homeless, the applicant is less able to fend for himself than an ordinary homeless person so as to suffer greater harm; medical evidence informs but does not determine the statutory question.
legal_issues: Correct application of Pereira and Osmani vulnerability tests
Whether use of 'peers' misstated the comparator group
Adequacy of inquiries including orthopaedic hospital report
Whether applicant should have been allowed to respond to Dr Keen's final report
linked_authorities: R v Camden LBC ex parte Pereira (1998) 31 HLR 317
Osmani v London Borough of Camden [2004] EWCA Civ 1706
R (Begum) v Tower Hamlets London Borough Council (2003) HLR 8

confidence.notes: Extensive factual medical history but appellate conclusions on law and review are clear.

notes: Footballer disability insurance appeal; normal ageing degeneration not excluded from policy construction.

enrichment.short_title: Blackburn Rovers v Avon Insurance: degenerative condition exclusion in player policy
key_facts: Blackburn Rovers claimed under a player disability policy after Martin Dahlin's spinal injury ended his career in October 1997.
Insurers relied on exclusion 4 excluding disablement attributable to arthritic or other degenerative conditions.
Moore-Bick J held normal age-related degeneration should be disregarded when construing the exclusion.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding causation not construction was central and normal degeneration could fall within the exclusion.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary issue trial on construction of an exclusion in a professional footballer permanent total disablement policy.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; negative answer to whether typical age-related degenerative changes should be disregarded for policy purposes.
enrichment.ratio: Disablement is not attributable to a pre-existing degenerative condition unless that condition is at least a causa sine qua non; the exclusion need not be read to ignore normal degeneration, and proximate cause principles govern whether exclusion 4 applies.
legal_issues: Construction of exclusion 4 for arthritic or degenerative conditions
Whether normal ageing degeneration falls outside the exclusion
Application of proximate cause in personal accident policies
Whether preliminary issue on construction was appropriate
linked_authorities: Yorkshire Water Services Ltd v Sun Alliance and London Insurance plc [1991] 2 Lloyd's Rep 21
Winspear v Accident Insurance Co (1880) 6 QBD 42

confidence.notes: Appellate reasoning overturning construction issue is clear though underlying causation facts remain disputed.
